content: After the publication of a study, when other research groups attempted and failed to replicate its findings, the International Committee for Medical Journal Editors emphasized their responsibility to investigate allegations of scientific misconduct. A study published in the peer-reviewed journal The Lancet, which claimed that long-term use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) was associated with a reduced risk of oral cancer, was later revealed to be entirely fabricated. Following this revelation, the journal issued a retraction and acknowledged that the study contained falsified data. Although it is often argued that fraud cannot be detected during the peer review process, the Journal of Cell Biology employs an image screening process that it asserts could have identified the manipulated figures published in Science by Woo-Suk Hwang. Instances of plagiarism among historians have been widely publicized. A survey of 3,247 scientists funded by the U.S. National Institutes of Health revealed that 0.3% admitted to fabricating data, 1.4% admitted to plagiarism, and 4.7% admitted to self-plagiarism. Self-plagiarism occurs when an author republishes the same material or data without citing their earlier work. Authors often engage in self-plagiarism to inflate their list of publications. Reviewers sometimes detect potential cases of plagiarism and report them to the editor. While reviewers generally lack access to raw data, they do have access to the full manuscript text, making them better positioned to identify plagiarism or self-plagiarism in prose than fraudulent data. Despite being more common than plagiarism, self-plagiarism is often not penalized by journals or employers. However, it violates the policies of most peer-reviewed journals, which typically require that only unpublished material be submitted. A related form of professional misconduct involves reviewers exploiting unpublished information from manuscripts or grant applications for personal or professional gain. The frequency of such occurrences is unknown, but the U.S. Office of Research Integrity has sanctioned reviewers caught engaging in this behavior. Authors can defend against this misconduct by pre-publishing their work as a preprint or technical report on public platforms like arXiv, which can later be used to establish priority. Traditional anonymous peer review has been criticized for its lack of accountability, potential for reviewer abuse, and susceptibility to bias and inconsistency. In response, alternative peer review systems with varying degrees of openness have been proposed. In 1996, the Journal of Interactive Media in Education introduced open peer review, where reviewers' names are disclosed, making them accountable for their reviews while also acknowledging their contributions. Authors are granted the right to respond, and other researchers can comment before publication. In 1999, the open-access Journal of Medical Internet Research began publishing reviewers' names at the end of each article. Similarly, the British Medical Journal (BMJ) adopted an open peer review system, revealing reviewers' identities to authors but not to readers. The BMC series of medical journals, launched in 2000, also implemented open peer review, publishing reviewers' names and making peer review reports available online as part of the pre-publication history. Evidence regarding the impact of open peer review on review quality, tone, and time spent is mixed. However, under open peer review, more invited reviewers decline to participate. In 2006, Nature experimented with parallel open peer review, allowing some articles to undergo both traditional anonymous review and open public commentary. The results were underwhelming, with only 5% of authors agreeing to participate and only 54% of those articles receiving comments. Editors speculated that researchers were too busy or reluctant to make their names public, and the simultaneous anonymous review process may have influenced participation. In 2006, the online journal Philica was launched to address issues with traditional peer review. Unlike conventional journals, all submitted articles are published immediately, and the review process occurs afterward. Reviews remain anonymous, but any researcher can review an article. Reviews are displayed at the end of each article, providing readers with criticism or guidance rather than determining publication. This approach prevents reviewers from suppressing ideas they disagree with. Another dynamic peer review model is Naboj, which allows users to write reviews of preprints on arXiv.org. The system is modeled on platforms like Amazon, enabling users to evaluate both reviews and articles. With sufficient participation, this model aims to improve the quality of the review process. In 2006, the journal Biology Direct introduced an alternative peer review model. Authors must secure three editorial board members to review or solicit external reviews for their article. Unlike Philica, reviews are not anonymous, and no article is published without being reviewed. Authors can withdraw, revise, or publish their article despite critical comments, with all reviews and reviewers' names made publicly available. Open Peer Commentary extends peer review beyond publication, soliciting expert commentaries on published articles and encouraging authors to respond. The BMJ's Rapid Responses feature facilitates ongoing debate and criticism post-publication. By 2005, stricter criteria were enforced to manage the quality of these responses. Volunteer peer review of preprints has also been proposed as a way to improve the review process. Peer review is not limited to academic publishing; it is also used to enhance government policy.
